planting.note: Plant bulbs or bulbils in fall into a site that stays damp in spring and early summer, such as a streambank margin or seasonally irrigated bed; leave spent foliage until it yellows.

directions: A widespread Rocky Mountain and Great Basin meadow and streambank native with showy pink-purple umbels, this onion tolerates damp sites better than most ornamental alliums, making it good for pollinator meadows and native rain-garden margins. Some populations produce bulbils for easy increase, and clumps bulk up over a few seasons via offsets. A streambank margin or seasonally irrigated bed suits it well, since it need not be wet year-round.

planting.note: Plant paired egg-shaped bulbs in fall where the site gets a cold winter chill and excellent drainage during summer dormancy, tucked among rocks or at a dry meadow edge.

directions: A high-elevation western native found in the Sierra, Great Basin, and Rockies, this onion carries delicate pale-purple, six-tepaled flowers in loose umbels, good for rock gardens and alpine meadow plantings mimicking its yellow-pine, red-fir, and lodgepole understory habitat. It is adapted to montane soils that are damp in snowmelt season and bone-dry by midsummer. The crushed foliage carries a notably strong onion scent, useful for rodent-resistant bulb plantings.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall under dappled oak or digger pine shade in heavy clay or serpentine soil without compost amendment; withhold water completely once foliage yellows in late spring.

directions: A California endemic with distinctive magenta flowers whose inner three crinkled, cloth-textured tepals curl under, this onion offers a genuinely unusual bloom form among native alliums, suited to dry woodland-garden underplanting. It is a clay-and-serpentine specialist, so heavy, mineral soils are a feature, not a flaw — avoid amending with rich compost. Its crinkled inner tepals are best appreciated at close range, so plant along a path edge or in a container for a rock-garden display.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in full sun with gravelly, fast-draining soil; unlike most California native bulbs it tolerates an occasional summer soak without rotting, making it suitable for containers.

directions: A strikingly showy rose-pink coastal bluff species already popular in California native horticulture, this onion attracts dozens of native bee and butterfly species, making it a strong pollinator choice for coastal gardens. Because it comes from exposed sea cliffs, give it full sun and gravelly, fast-draining soil, but it will tolerate an occasional summer soak without rotting — a real advantage in mixed coastal borders. It performs well in containers, a good option for gardeners outside its narrow native coastal-bluff range.

planting.note: Plant rhizomatous bulb clusters in fall on a dry slope or ridge among chaparral or sage-scrub companions; avoid piling mulch against the bulbs.

directions: A Southern California chaparral and coastal-sage-scrub native with vivid red bulb skins and white-to-pink, dark-midveined flowers, this onion is documented to attract dozens of native bee species, making it a strong pollinator choice for dry Southern California gardens. It is tolerant of a wide range of soils but resents mulch piled against the bulbs, which can promote rot. The bright red bulb coats make this one of the more ornamental alliums to handle and divide, with clumps spreading gradually via rhizomatous offsets.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall into a rock-garden pocket or raised bed with mineral grit near, but not under, oak canopy; let it go fully dry and dormant in summer.

directions: Striking rose-purple to maroon flower clusters held just above two curved, scythe-shaped leaves make this a true rock-garden gem long grown by specialist bulb nurseries, serpentine-adapted and compact. This species wants sharp drainage and benefits from growing near, though not under the dense canopy of, oaks, whose leaf litter it seems to favor nutritionally in the wild from the Bay Area north into Oregon. Its compact scythe-shaped leaves and bright flower heads make it one of the better small alliums for trough or rock-garden display.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall on a dry, sunny slope with pine or fir leaf litter mixed into the soil to mimic its forest-floor habitat.

directions: Found through pine and fir forest from Washington to California and Nevada, this onion carries large pink-to-purple umbels of up to 50 flowers with dark-based tepals, giving strong summer color in dry montane garden settings where little else blooms. Unlike many spring-blooming western alliums, it flowers in summer, filling a bloom gap in a dry pine-woodland or rock-garden planting. It produces small daughter bulblets on short rhizomes, so an established clump will slowly colonize a gravelly bed.

planting.note: Plant small egg-shaped bulbs in fall into talus, scree, or a gritty raised bed; keep dry through summer dormancy to avoid the most common cause of bulb loss.

directions: One of the most diminutive native alliums, rarely over five inches tall, this onion carries pale pink, dark-midveined flowers ideal for scree beds, troughs, and xeriscape rock gardens where larger alliums would overwhelm the scale. Give this miniature species the sharpest drainage possible, mimicking its native rocky slopes and seasonally moist scablands. Its tiny scale makes it easy to lose in a mixed border, so it shows best in a dedicated rock garden, trough, or path-edge planting.
